outputs.L1: The present invention relates to a test system for multi-fuel, high-temperature fuel cells, which enables the direct use of carbon-based fuels, including anhydrous fuels, without promoting or limiting carbon deposition in the gas inlet and outlet ducts or in the anode flow channels. The system comprises a furnace (5) containing a reactor (4), the reactor comprising at least two interconnection plates and at least one fuel cell (15) positioned between two interconnection plates. One of the interconnection plates in contact with the fuel cell defines a cathodic side that receives an oxidizing gas, while the other interconnection plate in contact with the fuel cell defines an anodic side that receives a combustible gas. The system further comprises controlled means for gas feeding and exhaustion connected to the reactor (4). Each plate further comprises a plurality of flow channels (14) on its upper and lower surfaces, through which the oxidizing gas and the combustible gas pass to contact the electrodes of the fuel cell (15). The base, top, and interconnection plates are made of a zirconium oxide- or cerium oxide-based material doped with one or more oxides selected from yttria, scandia, calcia, gadolinia, samaria, alumina, and cobaltite, with the total amount of dopants being up to 20% by weight.

The invention concerns a testing apparatus for high-temperature fuel cells capable of operating with multiple fuels. The system enables carbon-based fuels, including anhydrous fuels, to be used directly, without encouraging or restricting carbon formation in the gas inlet and outlet passages or in the anode flow channels.

The system includes a furnace (5) that houses a reactor (4). The reactor is formed from at least two interconnection plates and at least one fuel cell (15) positioned between two of those plates. Of the interconnection plates that contact the fuel cell, one forms the cathode side and receives an oxidizing gas, while the other forms the anode side and receives a fuel gas.

The system also includes controlled gas supply and discharge means connected to the reactor (4). Each plate has multiple flow channels (14) on both its upper and lower surfaces. The oxidizing gas and the fuel gas travel through these flow channels (14) so that they come into contact with the electrodes of the fuel cell (15).

The base plate, top plate, and interconnection plates are made from a material based on zirconium oxide or cerium oxide, doped with one or more oxides selected from yttria, scandia, calcia, gadolinia, samaria, alumina, and cobaltite. The total dopant content is up to 20% by weight.
outputs.L3:
The invention relates to a test system for multi-fuel, high-temperature fuel cells, particularly fuel cells capable of directly utilizing carbon-based fuels, including anhydrous fuels. The system is intended for evaluating fuel cell performance under conditions in which a variety of combustible gases or vapors may be supplied to the anode side, while an oxidizing gas is supplied to the cathode side.

A key feature of the system is that it is designed so as not to artificially promote or suppress carbon deposition in the gas inlet ducts, gas outlet ducts, or anode flow channels. This is especially important when testing carbon-containing fuels, since carbon formation can significantly affect both the operation of the fuel cell and the interpretation of test results. By avoiding conditions or materials that would either encourage or inhibit carbon deposition in these regions, the system enables more representative testing of the intrinsic behavior of the fuel cell and fuel under high-temperature operating conditions.

The test system comprises a furnace in which a reactor is arranged. The reactor includes at least two interconnection plates and at least one fuel cell positioned between the interconnection plates. The interconnection plates define the respective gas environments and provide the necessary interfaces for introducing and distributing gases to the fuel cell during testing.

One of the interconnection plates functions as the cathodic-side interconnection plate and is configured to receive an oxidizing gas, such as air or oxygen-containing gas. The other interconnection plate functions as the anodic-side interconnection plate and is configured to receive a combustible gas, which may include carbon-based fuels and, in particular, anhydrous fuels. In this arrangement, the fuel cell is exposed on one side to the oxidizing gas and on the opposite side to the combustible gas, thereby allowing electrochemical testing under controlled high-temperature conditions.

The reactor further includes structural components such as a base plate, a top plate, and the interconnection plates. These components are made from materials based on doped zirconium oxide or doped cerium oxide. The dopants are present in a total amount of up to 20% by weight. The use of such ceramic oxide-based materials provides chemical and thermal compatibility with high-temperature fuel cell operation and helps maintain test conditions that do not unduly influence carbon deposition behavior in the gas supply, exhaust, or anode flow regions.
outputs.L4:
A test system is proposed for evaluating multi-fuel, high-temperature fuel cells capable of directly using carbon-based fuels. The system is particularly suitable for testing fuel cells that operate with combustible gases or vapors derived from hydrocarbons, alcohols, carbonaceous materials, or other carbon-containing fuels, including anhydrous fuels. It is designed to reproduce realistic operating conditions while allowing controlled study of fuel-cell performance, gas distribution, and carbon-deposition behavior during direct fuel operation.

The system includes a reactor positioned inside a furnace so that the fuel cell or fuel-cell test assembly can be maintained at the required high operating temperature. Within the reactor, interconnection plates are arranged to define and separate flow paths for oxidizing gas and combustible gas. These plates provide gas-distribution channels for supplying the oxidant to the cathode side and the fuel or combustible gas to the anode side of the fuel cell. The system also includes controlled gas-feeding devices, exhaust lines, and associated flow-control components so that the composition, flow rate, and removal of the gases can be accurately regulated during testing.

A key feature of the proposed system is the material selected for the interconnection plates and related gas-contacting components. The plates are formed from doped zirconium-oxide-based or cerium-oxide-based materials. These ceramic oxide materials are stable under high-temperature fuel-cell operating conditions and are compatible with oxidizing and reducing atmospheres. Their use helps prevent the test fixture itself from artificially influencing carbon formation in the fuel-delivery ducts or in the anode flow channels.

By avoiding materials that either promote carbon deposition or suppress it through catalytic effects, the system allows the behavior of the fuel cell to be evaluated more accurately. In conventional test arrangements, metallic or catalytically active components may alter the chemistry of carbon-containing fuels before they reach the anode, leading to misleading results. The proposed oxide-based plates reduce this interference, making it possible to determine whether carbon deposition is caused by the fuel, operating temperature, gas composition, or the fuel-cell electrode itself rather than by the test apparatus.

The system therefore provides a more reliable platform for studying direct carbon-fuel operation in high-temperature fuel cells, such as solid oxide fuel cells. It enables testing with a broad range of carbon-based fuels, including dry or anhydrous fuels, under controlled and repeatable conditions. As a result, it can be used to assess cell performance, durability, fuel utilization, carbon tolerance, and operating limits in a manner that more closely reflects the true behavior of the fuel-cell materials and design.
outputs.L5:
**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest words in English, but it plays a very important role. It is called the definite article, and it helps us talk about something specific. For example, when we say “a book,” we mean any book. But when we say “the book,” we mean a particular book that both the speaker and listener know about.

The word “the” gives meaning and direction to a sentence. It can point to something unique, such as “the sun,” “the moon,” or “the world.” It can also refer to something already mentioned: “I saw a dog. The dog was friendly.” In this case, “the” tells us that we are still talking about the same dog.

Although it is simple, “the” is one of the most common words in the English language. It appears in conversations, books, songs, news, and everyday writing. Without it, many sentences would sound unclear or unnatural.

In short, “the” may be a tiny word, but it has a big purpose. It helps make language more precise, clear, and meaningful.

counterfactuals.output:
**Patent Specification Excerpt**

In one embodiment, a multi-fuel solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) testing apparatus is provided for evaluating electrochemical performance under a plurality of fuel compositions while inhibiting or preventing carbon deposition within fuel gas ducts and anode flow channels. The apparatus comprises a fuel supply section, a humidification and reforming section, a heated fuel delivery section, a test fixture configured to receive at least one SOFC cell or stack, an oxidant supply section, and an exhaust and monitoring section.

The fuel supply section includes a plurality of fuel sources selectively coupled to the test fixture through respective mass-flow controllers. The plurality of fuel sources may include hydrogen, methane, natural gas, carbon monoxide, synthesis gas, ammonia-derived hydrogen, alcohol-derived reformate, hydrocarbon mixtures, or combinations thereof. A switching manifold is provided downstream of the fuel sources and is configured to permit controlled selection, blending, and transition between fuels without exposing the SOFC anode to carbon-forming conditions. The switching manifold may include purge-gas inlets, isolation valves, non-return valves, and a controller configured to coordinate valve actuation and flow rates.

The humidification and reforming section is disposed upstream of the SOFC test fixture and is configured to introduce a controlled quantity of steam into the fuel stream. In certain embodiments, the humidification and reforming section comprises a temperature-controlled evaporator, a steam generator, a water metering pump, and a mixing chamber. The controller maintains a steam-to-carbon ratio above a predetermined threshold selected to suppress pyrolysis, coking, and Boudouard carbon formation in hydrocarbon-containing fuel streams. The humidification and reforming section may further include a catalytic pre-reformer adapted to convert higher hydrocarbons into a reformate containing hydrogen, carbon monoxide, carbon dioxide, methane, and steam prior to introduction into the anode flow channels.

A heated fuel delivery section extends between the humidification and reforming section and the test fixture. The heated fuel delivery section includes one or more gas ducts, conduits, fittings, and manifolds maintained at an elevated temperature sufficient to prevent condensation of steam and heavy hydrocarbons and to reduce formation of solid carbon. In one embodiment, the gas ducts comprise inert or oxidation-resistant materials, including alumina, quartz, high-temperature stainless steel, nickel-based alloys, or ceramic-coated metal tubes. The ducts may include electrical trace heaters, radiant heaters, thermal insulation, and temperature sensors arranged along substantially the entire fuel path. The controller regulates the heaters to maintain a substantially uniform duct temperature and to avoid localized cold spots that would otherwise promote carbon deposition.

The test fixture includes an SOFC holder having an anode-side inlet manifold, an anode-side outlet manifold, a cathode-side inlet manifold, and a cathode-side outlet manifold. The SOFC holder is configured to seal against a planar cell, tubular cell, button cell, short stack, or other SOFC test article. The anode-side inlet manifold distributes the prepared fuel stream to one or more anode flow channels. The anode flow channels are dimensioned and arranged to provide substantially uniform fuel distribution and to minimize stagnant regions in which carbonaceous deposits may accumulate. In selected embodiments, the anode flow channels include rounded transitions, reduced dead volumes, smooth internal surfaces, or coatings resistant to carbon nucleation.

A carbon-deposition prevention assembly is operatively associated with the fuel delivery section and the anode-side components. The carbon-deposition prevention assembly includes at least one of: a steam addition device, a carbon dioxide addition device, a controlled oxygen or air bleed device, a catalytic reforming element, a purge-gas supply, and a temperature-control system. The controlled oxygen or air bleed device may be configured to introduce a sub-stoichiometric amount of oxidant sufficient to promote partial oxidation or gasification of carbon precursors without damaging the anode. The purge-gas supply may provide nitrogen, argon, steam, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, or mixtures thereof during start-up, shut-down, and fuel-transition operations.

In one embodiment, the controller is programmed to execute a carbon-suppression operating protocol. The protocol comprises heating the gas ducts and anode manifolds to a predetermined minimum temperature before introduction of hydrocarbon fuel; initiating flow of steam, hydrogen, carbon dioxide, or another non-coking gas prior to hydrocarbon admission; maintaining the fuel mixture outside a carbon-forming region as determined by temperature, pressure, steam-to-carbon ratio, oxygen-to-carbon ratio, and fuel composition; and purging the anode flow channels following interruption or termination of hydrocarbon fuel flow. The controller may further receive input from temperature sensors, pressure sensors, humidity sensors, oxygen sensors, hydrocarbon sensors, and gas analyzers positioned upstream and downstream of the test fixture.

The apparatus may include a diagnostic section comprising one or more sampling ports, gas chromatographs, mass spectrometers, infrared analyzers, dew-point sensors, or electrochemical sensors for determining the composition of inlet and outlet gases. The diagnostic section enables detection of carbon-forming precursors and adjustment of operating parameters in response thereto. A pressure-regulation system may also be provided to maintain desired pressure differentials across the cell while preventing backflow of oxidant into the anode-side fuel ducts.

The exhaust and monitoring section includes heated exhaust lines connected to the anode outlet manifold and cathode outlet manifold. The heated exhaust lines are maintained above a condensation temperature of water and hydrocarbons to reduce accumulation of liquids or carbonaceous residues. The anode exhaust line may include a combustor, flare, catalytic oxidizer, condenser located downstream of a heated section, and flow-measurement device. In some embodiments, a portion of the anode exhaust is recycled to the fuel inlet to increase steam, carbon dioxide, or hydrogen concentration and thereby suppress carbon deposition.

Accordingly, the multi-fuel SOFC testing apparatus permits testing with hydrogen-containing, carbon monoxide-containing, and hydrocarbon-containing fuels while reducing or eliminating carbon deposition in gas ducts and anode flow channels. The combination of controlled humidification, pre-reforming, heated delivery conduits, purge capability, fuel-transition control, and real-time monitoring maintains the fuel stream in a thermodynamic and kinetic regime unfavorable to carbon formation during steady-state operation, start-up, shut-down, and transitions between fuels.

counterfactuals.output:
## Technical Description

A high-temperature fuel cell test reactor is provided for operation within a furnace and for evaluating multi-fuel electrochemical cells under controlled thermal and gas-atmosphere conditions. The reactor comprises a furnace-compatible reactor body configured to house at least one high-temperature fuel cell specimen, such as a solid oxide fuel cell, protonic ceramic fuel cell, mixed ionic-electronic conducting cell, or related electrochemical device having an anode side and a cathode side.

In one embodiment, the reactor body is formed from an oxidation-resistant and high-temperature-stable material, including but not limited to alumina, mullite, zirconia, quartz, high-temperature alloy, or combinations thereof. The reactor body is dimensioned for placement inside a tube furnace, box furnace, split furnace, vertical furnace, or other controlled heating apparatus capable of maintaining operating temperatures in the range of about 400°C to about 1,200°C, preferably about 600°C to about 1,000°C for high-temperature fuel cell testing.

### Anode and Cathode Chambers

The reactor includes an anode chamber and a cathode chamber separated by the fuel cell under test. The fuel cell is mounted such that a first surface of the cell is exposed to an anode-side gas stream and a second opposing surface is exposed to a cathode-side gas stream. The anode side is configured to receive fuel gases, reformate gases, or mixtures thereof, while the cathode side is configured to receive oxidant gases.

The anode chamber may be supplied with one or more fuels selected from hydrogen, carbon monoxide, methane, ethane, propane, butane, natural gas, syngas, ammonia, methanol vapor, ethanol vapor, hydrocarbons, humidified fuels, dry fuels, inert carrier gas mixtures, or combinations thereof. The cathode chamber may be supplied with air, oxygen, oxygen-enriched air, carbon dioxide-containing oxidant streams, nitrogen-diluted oxidant streams, steam-containing oxidants, or combinations thereof.

A seal assembly is positioned between the anode chamber and cathode chamber to inhibit gas cross-leakage. The seal assembly may include glass-ceramic seals, mica seals, compressive gaskets, ceramic fiber seals, metal brazes, compliant ceramic seals, or combinations thereof. In certain embodiments, the reactor includes a clamping fixture or spring-loaded compression assembly to maintain sealing force during thermal cycling.

### Gas Inlet and Outlet Control

The reactor includes independently controllable gas inlet and outlet connections for the anode side and cathode side. In one embodiment, an anode inlet conduit is fluidly connected to the anode chamber and an anode outlet conduit is fluidly connected downstream of the anode chamber. A cathode inlet conduit is fluidly connected to the cathode chamber and a cathode outlet conduit is fluidly connected downstream of the cathode chamber.

Each inlet may be connected to a gas delivery manifold including one or more mass flow controllers, pressure regulators, check valves, shutoff valves, humidifiers, bubblers, evaporators, reformers, preheaters, or gas-mixing units. Each outlet may include one or more pressure-control devices, condensers, filters, exhaust traps, back-pressure regulators, gas analyzers, sampling ports, flow meters, flame arrestors, or ventilation connections.

The anode inlet and cathode inlet are preferably controlled independently to allow separate adjustment of gas composition, flow rate, humidity, pressure, and temperature. The anode outlet and cathode outlet may likewise be independently controlled to regulate residence time, outlet pressure, fuel utilization, oxidant utilization, and exhaust composition. In one embodiment, the reactor is configured to operate with counter-flow, co-flow, or cross-flow gas arrangements between the anode and cathode sides.

### Flow Channel Configuration

At least one flow-field member is disposed adjacent to the anode side, the cathode side, or both sides of the fuel cell. The flow-field member includes a plurality of flow channels configured to distribute gas substantially uniformly across an active area of the fuel cell. The flow channels may be straight, serpentine, interdigitated, radial, spiral, parallel, tapered, manifolded, or combinations thereof.

In an exemplary configuration, the anode-side flow-field member includes a plurality of fuel flow channels extending from an anode inlet manifold to an anode outlet manifold. The cathode-side flow-field member includes a plurality of oxidant flow channels extending from a cathode inlet manifold to a cathode outlet manifold. The channels may be formed by machining, casting, extrusion, additive manufacturing, laser cutting, etching, pressing, or ceramic molding.

The flow channels may have rectangular, semicircular, trapezoidal, triangular, or rounded cross-sections. Channel depth, width, spacing, and length may be selected to provide desired pressure drop, gas distribution, and reactant utilization. In one embodiment, channel dimensions range from about 0.1 mm to about 10 mm in width and about 0.05 mm to about 5 mm in depth. The flow-field member may be made from alumina, zirconia, lanthanum chromite, stainless steel, nickel alloy, ferritic alloy, coated metal, electrically conductive ceramic, or composite material.

### Multi-Fuel Testing Capability

The reactor is configured for multi-fuel operation by allowing rapid or programmable switching between different anode gas compositions while maintaining stable cathode flow. A multi-port gas manifold may be coupled to the anode inlet and configured to selectively deliver hydrogen, hydrocarbon fuel, ammonia, syngas, alcohol vapor, inert purge gas, or mixtures thereof. The manifold may include automated valves controlled by a programmable controller to execute fuel-switching sequences, redox cycling protocols, start-up procedures, shutdown procedures, and safety purging.

In certain embodiments, the anode-side gas stream is passed through a humidification module or vapor generator before entering the furnace. The reactor may include heated gas lines or internal preheating sections to prevent condensation and to deliver reactants at a controlled temperature. Optional reforming catalysts may be provided upstream of the anode chamber or within the anode-side flow field to partially or fully reform hydrocarbon or alcohol fuels before electrochemical reaction.

### Electrical and Diagnostic Connections

The reactor may include electrical current collectors positioned in contact with the anode and cathode sides of the fuel cell. The current collectors may comprise platinum mesh, gold mesh, nickel mesh, silver mesh, stainless steel mesh, lanthanum strontium manganite, lanthanum strontium cobalt ferrite, conductive ceramic, conductive coating, or combinations thereof. Electrical leads extend from the current collectors through furnace-compatible feedthroughs to external instrumentation for measuring voltage, current, impedance, power density, polarization behavior, open-circuit voltage, degradation rate, and fuel utilization.

The reactor may further include thermocouples positioned adjacent to the fuel cell, at inlet and outlet gas regions, or within the furnace hot zone. Pressure sensors, oxygen sensors, humidity sensors, gas chromatograph sampling ports, mass spectrometer ports, or infrared gas analysis ports may be connected to the anode outlet, cathode outlet, or both.

### Ceramic Materials and Dopants

The reactor is suitable for testing cells including ceramic electrolyte, electrode, barrier, interlayer, catalyst, or support materials containing one or more dopants. The ceramic materials may include zirconia-based ceramics, ceria-based ceramics, barium zirconate, barium cerate, lanthanum gallate, perovskite oxides, fluorite oxides, spinel oxides, pyrochlore oxides, proton-conducting ceramics, oxygen-ion-conducting ceramics, mixed conducting ceramics, or composite ceramic-metal materials.

Dopants may be incorporated in an amount up to about 20 wt% based on the total weight of the respective ceramic phase. Suitable dopants include, but are not limited to, yttrium, scandium, ytterbium, gadolinium, samarium, neodymium, praseodymium, lanthanum, cerium, calcium, magnesium, strontium, barium, cobalt, iron, nickel, copper, manganese, aluminum, gallium, indium, titanium, niobium, tantalum, tungsten, molybdenum, chromium, vanadium, or combinations thereof.

In one embodiment, an electrolyte comprises yttria-stabilized zirconia, scandia-stabilized zirconia, gadolinia-doped ceria, samaria-doped ceria, yttrium-doped barium zirconate, yttrium-doped barium cerate-zirconate, or lanthanum gallate doped with strontium and magnesium. In another embodiment, an electrode comprises nickel-ceria, nickel-zirconia, lanthanum strontium manganite, lanthanum strontium cobalt ferrite, lanthanum strontium ferrite, barium strontium cobalt ferrite, or doped perovskite materials containing one or more dopants up to about 20 wt%.

The dopants may be selected to modify ionic conductivity, electronic conductivity, catalytic activity, thermal expansion coefficient, sintering behavior, phase stability, redox tolerance, sulfur tolerance, carbon deposition resistance, mechanical strength, or chemical compatibility with adjacent cell layers.

### Furnace Integration

The reactor is configured to be positioned within a furnace hot zone such that the fuel cell is maintained at a substantially uniform temperature during testing. The gas inlet conduits may extend through one side of the furnace and the gas outlet conduits through the same or opposite side. In one embodiment, inlet gases are preheated by passage through heated conduit sections located within the furnace before entering the respective anode or cathode flow channels.

The reactor body may include alignment structures, spacers, compression plates, insulating members, or support fixtures to maintain the cell in a fixed position during heating, cooling, and gas switching. The reactor may be configured for horizontal or vertical orientation and may accommodate button cells, planar cells, tubular cells, segmented cells, microtubular cells, electrolyte-supported cells, anode-supported cells, metal-supported cells, or cathode-supported cells.

### Exemplary Claim-Style Statement

A furnace-insertable reactor for testing a multi-fuel high-temperature fuel cell comprises: a reactor housing configured for placement within a furnace; a fuel cell mounting region configured to receive a fuel cell having an anode side and a cathode side; an anode chamber disposed adjacent to the anode side; a cathode chamber disposed adjacent to the cathode side; an anode gas inlet and an anode gas outlet in fluid communication with the anode chamber; a cathode gas inlet and a cathode gas outlet in fluid communication with the cathode chamber; independently controllable gas delivery and exhaust control components connected to the anode and cathode gas inlets and outlets; and one or more flow-field members defining gas flow channels for distributing fuel gas and oxidant gas over respective active surfaces of the fuel cell, wherein the reactor is configured to test ceramic fuel cell materials containing one or more dopants in an amount up to about 20 wt% based on the ceramic phase.
